Programming Language Characteristics: Cardano Aiken
For fine-tuning a LLM to generate Cardano Aiken smart contract code, we need to define the key characteristics of the programming language. Here's a breakdown of the features and characteristics of Cardano Aiken that have been targeted:
Syntax*
Functional programming: Aiken is a functional programming language, which means it emphasises the use of pure functions, immutability, and recursion.
Aiken's syntax has a focus on concise and expressive code.
Semantics
Strongly typed: Aiken is a statically typed language, which means that the type system checks the types of variables at compile-time, preventing type errors at runtime.
Type inference: Aiken's type system can infer the types of variables, reducing the need for explicit type annotations.
Referential transparency: Aiken's functional programming model ensures that functions have no side effects, making it easier to reason about code.
Type Systems
Type classes: Aiken's type system includes type classes, which enable more modular and reusable code.
Execution Models
EUTxO (Extended UTXO) model: Aiken is designed to work with the eUTxO model, which is a variant of the UTXO (Unspent Transaction Output) model used in Bitcoin. The LLM will be fine tuned to also understand the eUTxO model.
Smart Contract Specifics
On-chain execution: Aiken smart contracts are executed on the Cardano blockchain, which means that the LLM should be able to generate code that interacts with the blockchain and specific Cardano Validator actions.

Objectives of Milestone 2
1. Evaluation of a suitable Large Language Model (LLM) base model for fine-tuning, that can generate Aiken code.
2. Perform initial fine-tuning with the custom training dataset from Milestone 1.
a. Test model after fine-tuning and ensure it is ready for full scale testing deployment and initial feedback.
3. Fine-tuning and dataset with improved dataset after testing and initial feedback. The aim being to reduce over fitting and improving performance on Aiken syntax and capabilities.
a. Inference on local machine should be at an acceptable and of a speed of less than a few seconds.
4. Start testing first version and fully deploy to testers with instructions on how to install, use and expectations.
 
Aiken Version Changes Identified
Aiken version 1 came out of Beta in Sept 2024, this was at the same time as Plutus V3. Various language changes have been added to Aiken V1 that differ from the Beta version. These differences restrict the amount of mainnet Aiken v1 code the LLM can be trained on. The initial fine tune will use as much Aiken code as possible to train the LLM regardless of versions.
While researching the Aiken code repositories on GitHub it was noted there is also a limited supply of real world Aiken code to fine tune the LLM on. The aim will be to fill these gaps after initial testing by generating synthetic data based on Aiken V1 to further enhance the LLM in areas that are lacking. Due to significant syntax changes only the recent versions of Aiken that were developed with the Stdlib 2.1 were used from GitHub in the final custom training dataset.

Key Performance Indicators (KPI) were -
1. Generate an Aiken smart code dataset using available data
1) Fine tuning of an open source LLM with Aiken smart code training dataset
2) Evaluation of fine-tuned LLM to analyse Aiken smart code
3) Evaluation of fine-tuned LLM to generate Aiken smart code

1- Fine tuning of an open source LLM with Aiken smart code training dataset 
How was KPI 1 addressed -
Aiken smart code documentation was extracted from the web plus all examples from GitHub for the latest Aiken standard library version 2.1.
The following script was used to extract code from GitHub –
https://github.com/jest-aiken-code/google-colab-python/blob/main/extractGitHubAikenCode.py
It should be noted that presently there is only a limited amount of Aiken code. A python batch script was developed to extract Aiken projects from GitHub, however at times the code libraries were found to be mixed. To ensure more accuracy with code generation more code examples are required to build a complete and robust dataset, in the end we had approximately 9000 examples of codes.
The final dataset was mostly hand checked along with additional data scraped and added from documentation plus various synthetic data examples were generated. The final dataset was uploaded onto Huggingface.co here -
https://huggingface.co/datasets/AmiBening/cardano-aiken-stdlib-v2-1
An appropriate LLM was chosen as the base LLM to fine tune the dataset with, after a selection process Qwen 2.5 was settled upon and within that after more testing the Qwen 2.5 Coder model was chosen. The following table shows other LLMs considered that were –
